record.name: HBM silicon intensity and allocation
record.role: Estimates wafer demand per delivered bit without double-counting embedded yield losses.
record.description: HBM requires silicon for memory arrays, peripheral circuits, vertical connections and base-die functions, followed by thinning, stacking and test. A stack’s footprint hides the area of its multiple dies. Silicon intensity can mean geometric area per bit or empirical wafer supply per delivered bit: different accounting methods. The geometric route explicitly applies relevant yields. An empirical ratio may already include those losses and must not receive them again. This lesson converts memory requirements into a consistent supply boundary with a dated supplier comparison whose denominator is kept explicit.

specs.label: Geometric method
specs.value: Area per gross bit plus explicit yields
specs.context: Separate memory and logic-process base-die wafer requirements.

specs.label: Empirical method
specs.context: State generation, node, output boundary and included losses.

specs.label: Different quantities
specs.value: Footprint, summed silicon area and delivered capacity
specs.context: Stack height and package area alone cannot measure wafer demand.

interfaces.name: Memory requirement and scoped model
interfaces.signal: Target bits, product configuration and nonoverlapping yield/intensity assumptions

interfaces.name: Normalized manufacturing demand
interfaces.signal: Wafer-equivalent or good-stack requirements over a stated period

record.tradeoff: More capacity or bandwidth can consume additional wafer and assembly resources; architecture and memory-traffic improvements can reduce demand.
record.whyAI: HBM can limit deployable accelerators even when logic wafers are available, connecting model memory requirements to manufacturing allocation.

record.scale: Memory channels, package links and wafer-supply accounting
record.subbranch: HBM interfaces, generations and silicon intensity
mechanism: Specify gross, good-die, tested-stack or package-delivered bits as the output boundary.
For geometry, sum die area and apply explicitly defined, nonoverlapping yield losses.
For empirical intensity, determine which wafer-to-output losses the reported ratio already includes.
Calculate separate memory and base-die process demands without applying any loss twice.
Compare stack demand with logic, substrate and assembly constraints before predicting delivered accelerators.
record.misconception: Wafer-supply intensity is neither package footprint nor a universal multiplier across HBM generations.

check.question: When is applying an extra stack-yield penalty to an empirical wafer/output-bit ratio justified?
options: Never for any geometric model either
Only when that ratio demonstrably excludes the stack loss
Always, because more factors improve accuracy
check.explanation: The starting metric’s denominator and included losses determine which additional factors are legitimate.

science.title: Two alternative demand models
science.equation: Geometric: W ≈ B_target a_bit/(A_usable Y); empirical: W = B_target I_emp
science.explanation: B_target is target output bits, a_bit gross silicon area/bit, A_usable effective wafer area, Y the explicitly modeled nonoverlapping survival, and I_emp wafers/output bit.
science.assumptions: Account separately for packing, redundancy and logic-process base dies; do not combine these alternative formulas blindly.

record.learningObjective: Choose a consistent HBM silicon-intensity method and avoid duplicated yield penalties.
record.engineeringExample: Synthetic empirical case: two wafer-equivalents per unit of tested-stack bits and ten units of demand require twenty wafer-equivalents. Applying a stack yield already embedded in that intensity would overstate demand.
record.evidenceNotes: Micron’s March 20, 2024 prepared remarks, page 6, report approximately 3× wafer supply for HBM3E versus DDR5 at equal bits and the same technology node. The original PDF was recovered from Micron’s legacy investor-relations host on September 7, 2026. This historical supplier statement does not establish a universal generation-independent factor, package footprint or current customer allocation. The lab keeps synthetic inputs and does not add losses already embedded in an empirical ratio.
record.scope: Compare a synthetic geometric area ratio with an output-normalized supply ratio without applying the same yield loss twice.
record.labScope: Compare a synthetic geometric area ratio with an output-normalized supply ratio without applying the same yield loss twice.

variables.meaning: Wafer requirement under the selected alternative model
Gross silicon area per bit under the geometric convention
Explicit nonoverlapping survival fraction excluded from a_bit
Empirical wafer requirement per delivered output bit

formalEquations.text: The geometric model divides target bits times gross area per bit by usable wafer area and an explicitly separate survival fraction. The alternative empirical model multiplies target output bits by measured wafers per output bit.
formalEquations.note: These are alternative models. An empirical output-bit intensity may already include yield; do not add the same loss again.

claims.title: Historical HBM3E wafer-supply comparison
claims.statement: In its March 20, 2024 prepared remarks, Micron reported that HBM3E needed approximately three times DDR5 wafer supply for equal bit output at the same technology node.
claims.denominator: Equal bit output at the same technology node
claims.limitations: Historical manufacturer-reported comparison, not an independent wafer-fab measurement. The remarks do not itemize individual die, stacking or test losses; do not apply those again without a separate boundary. It is neither package footprint nor a universal multiplier for all HBM generations, and no production lab default is inferred.
